Short, plain definitions for the terms used in the GEN series. If a term is missing, it should be added here with a one-line definition and linked from the article that uses it.
AADC (aromatic L-amino acid decarboxylase; gene DDC)
The enzyme that turns L-DOPA into dopamine
One version of a gene or DNA variant. You have two copies of most genes, one from each parent
One changed copy is enough to cause the condition
Two changed copies are needed; parents are usually unaffected carriers
Deep brain structures involved in movement and habit, and heavily dependent on dopamine
A helper molecule that tyrosine hydroxylase needs to make L-DOPA. The enzyme GCH1 controls the rate-limiting step of making it
A gene chosen in advance because it seemed plausible. Studies of candidate genes are older and less reliable than genome-wide ones
Someone who has a changed copy of a gene
A stretch of DNA that is missing or repeated
New in a person, not inherited from either parent
DAT (dopamine transporter; gene SLC6A3, old name DAT1)
The protein that pulls dopamine back into the cell after release
The list of conditions a clinician is weighing and needs to rule in or out
Sustained or repeated muscle contractions that cause twisting movements or abnormal postures
A group of conditions, often involving the GCH1 or TH genes, in which symptoms improve markedly with low-dose levodopa
The gene in a risk region that is thought to actually drive the effect. Proposed by computer methods and needs confirmation
The protein-coding parts of the genome
How strongly or in what way a variant shows up in a person
A study that scans the whole genome in many people to find common DNA differences linked to a trait
The proportion of differences in a trait across a population that is explained by genetic differences. It is not the proportion of any one person's condition
Having one changed copy and one typical copy of a gene
Having two identical copies of a variant
A group of inherited conditions causing progressive stiffness and weakness in the legs
An underlying tendency toward a condition, spread across a population. Diagnosis is thought of as the point where liability passes a threshold
The precursor that the body converts to dopamine. Used as a medicine and as a diagnostic clue
Enzymes that break down dopamine and related chemicals
The share of carriers who develop the condition. "Reduced penetrance" means some carriers never do
The study of how genes change the way the body handles a drug
Influenced by many genes, each with a small effect
A number that adds up many small DNA effects into one risk estimate for a person
The first person in a family to be identified with a condition
The slowest step in a chain, which sets the pace of the whole pathway
A change in a single DNA letter that is common in the population
The share of heritability explained by common variants
Muscle stiffness caused by a fault in the nervous-system control of muscle tone, often with exaggerated reflexes
The rate-limiting enzyme in dopamine production
A child and both parents sequenced together, to find new (
Comparing identical with non-identical twins to estimate how much of a trait is genetic
A pump that uses ATP to build a proton gradient across a vesicle's membrane. VMAT2 uses that gradient to pack dopamine into the vesicle
A difference in DNA from the typical sequence
The protein that loads dopamine, serotonin and noradrenaline into storage vesicles
A stretch of DNA made of a repeating unit. The number of repeats varies between people. DAT1 and DRD4 have well-known ones
A DNA change where there is not enough evidence to call it harmful or harmless. Not a diagnosis
A tiny bubble inside a nerve cell that stores chemical messengers ready for release
